sections.html:
• Common names: freshwater mussels, basket clams, Asian clams, Asiatic clams
  • Scientific name: Corbicula spp.
  • Minimum tank size: 40 litres
  • Keeping: easy-medium; breeding: medium
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: algae eater/omnivore (filter-feeding)
  • Temperament: peaceful and solitary
  • Colour: golden tan, light or dark brown

Freshwater clams are affordable. The average purchase size is typically 1.5–2.5 cm in diameter. Look for thick, ridged shells free of chips, cracks or holes, in golden tan, light brown or dark brown; white streaks or a little green algae coating are common. Healthy clams close their shells when poked, so checking for shell movement improves the chance of choosing healthy specimens.

Freshwater clams are bivalve mollusks of the order Venerida, family Corbiculidae (also known as Cyrenidae), commonly called basket clams because of their concentric-ribbed shells. The genus Corbicula comprises freshwater and brackish-water clams native to East Asia. Corbicula fluminalis and Corbicula fluminea are the species most widely used in aquariums, which is why they are collectively called "Asian or Asiatic clams". In Southeast Asia they are known as golden clam, prosperity clam, pygmy clam or good luck clam.

Corbicula are native to East Asia, occurring in rivers, streams and lakes in China, Japan, Taiwan, the Philippines and parts of South Korea. As an introduced/invasive species they are present in South America, North America, western and eastern Europe and North Africa, so they are found on every continent except Antarctica.

Freshwater clams of the family Corbiculidae are usually golden tan, light or dark brown, sometimes with irregular white streaks. The shell measures about 5–7 cm. This calcareous shell is divided into two valves, commonly of equal size, held together at the hinge by a ligament which also allows it to open. It closes tightly through the contraction of two adductor muscles. The clam has a powerful, muscular burrowing foot that lets it bury itself in the substrate for extended periods. Inside the shell are soft tissue, typically off-white or slightly pink, and siphons responsible for water passage, respiration and suspension-feeding. Depending on the species, lifespan ranges between 1 and 5 years.

Taxonomy at species level is very difficult, with more than 460 freshwater clam species. Corbicula fluminea and Corbicula fluminalis are often confused, but can be told apart by the number of ribs on the shell: C. fluminea has 7–14 ribs per centimetre, while C. fluminalis has 13–28. C. fluminalis is said to be rounder, whereas C. fluminea is slightly flatter.

Keep freshwater clams in a tank of at least 40 litres; anything smaller causes problems because of their unique feeding behaviour. Larger tanks help keep water chemistry stable and allow several clams to be kept together, so tanks larger than 80 litres are preferable.

Freshwater clams are an obligate filter-feeder, so they need plenty of particulate matter, phytoplankton and suspended detritus in the water. Do not treat them like snails (drop and forget). Lack of food, poor acclimation or large swings in parameters can kill a clam and release large amounts of ammonia into the tank.

Test the water regularly to keep ammonia, nitrite and nitrate in check, and do partial water changes of at least 20% every two weeks. Do not use copper-based medications; if necessary, move the clams to a separate tank and return them only after the copper has been completely removed by chemical filtration. Acclimate them properly before adding.

Check them from time to time by gently tapping the shell: a healthy clam moves or closes its shell quickly, while a dead one does not respond. A shell slightly ajar is fine, but too wide open is a sign of death. A dead clam smells awful (like rotten eggs). Remove a dead clam quickly, because it causes an ammonia spike that can ruin the tank.

Corbicula tolerate desiccation when low temperature and high humidity coincide, but not at high temperatures: 100% mortality was recorded after 48 hours at 25 and 30 °C for Corbicula fluminea.

Temperature: ideally 18–26 °C. They prefer cooler water. Their temperature tolerance is widely reported as 2–36 °C, and they showed 75% survival when exposed to 0 °C water for up to 4 weeks.

pH: best at 7.0–8.0. They can tolerate pH 6.5 and lower, but should not be left in acidic water for weeks, as acidic water slowly dissolves the shell. The harder the water, the better for the shell.

Hardness: 5–20 dKH helps maintain a healthy shell.

Corbicula can live in fresh and brackish water with salinity up to 10–17 ppm. Keep nitrate below 20 ppm.

Clams are sensitive to copper, especially if tap water contains it. Acclimate them carefully before adding them to the tank.

Lighting: not high, but bright enough to support the growth of their food, green water algae. Remove any UV sterilizer from the tank. LED lighting or T5/T8 bulbs can be used, for at least 8 hours daily.

Substrate: a fine substrate such as sand, in a layer of at least 5 cm so the clams can burrow.

Water flow: a well-oxygenated tank with moderate water flow helps them filter large amounts of particulate matter and plankton. Low flow and low dissolved oxygen are related to high mortality. The current should be neither too slow nor too fast; if possible, place them where water moves steadily.

Plants: clams do not eat healthy plants, but their burrowing can displace some plants. Floating plants, plants that do not need substrate (Anubias, Java fern, Java moss, Marimo moss balls, Subwassertang) or artificial plants are the best choice.

The main diet is particulate matter and suspended microalgae, filtered from the water column with paired siphons. The aquarium water should contain plenty of tiny debris, detritus and decaying matter, as clams do not like tanks that are "too clean".

They can also feed on detritus on the bottom (pedal feeding), but it is not their favourite way. If they do this regularly, there is not enough current or food in the current, and this should be corrected.

They readily accept powdered foods such as spirulina powder, zooplankton, Golden Pearls of 5–50 micron size, phytoplankton and powdered rotifers. In an emergency, finely crushed flakes, pellets and algae wafers can be used.

Feed 2–3 times a week. If clams stop accepting food, check whether a curious or nippy tank mate is bothering them, as they will not feed when agitated. Offer calcium supplements to strengthen the shell.

Freshwater clams are peaceful and solitary and will not harm fish or invertebrates. They embed themselves partially or completely in fine sand, spending much of their time buried; at other times they move briefly around the tank or rest on top of the substrate.

They filter large amounts of water to feed and breathe, which promotes water clarity; there are cases of clams clearing green water within short periods. Growth is slow but steady if they are healthy and well fed.

Tank mates: they suit a community tank with calm, peaceful fish (e.g. panda garra, pygmy corydoras, otocinclus). Do not keep them with puffers, cichlids, loaches or other aggressive fish. Good shrimp companions are those that prefer slightly alkaline water (vampire, bamboo, Amano, ghost, cherry, blue tiger, snowball shrimp, Caridina cf. babaulti, blue velvet, Malawa). Snails such as black devil, Brotia pagodula, rabbit, nerite, mystery, ramshorn and Malaysian trumpet snails are fine. Keep them away from all crayfish (even dwarf Mexican crayfish), most freshwater crabs and predatory shrimp such as Macrobrachium, which can be very aggressive towards clams.

Under optimal conditions, Corbicula clams breed in the aquarium. They are self-fertile simultaneous hermaphrodites, producing sperm that fertilizes the eggs internally. Most larval development occurs in the gills and body cavity of the adult. These features, along with early maturation (3–6 months), contribute to their successful invasion of new habitats. Corbicula can release up to 570 mucoid larvae per day per individual, and more than 68,000 per year. The larvae metamorphose into juveniles and then adults.

Warning: some clams produce microscopic larvae that attach to fish gills (potentially causing whirling disease) and later drop off. Do not collect freshwater clams from local ponds or rivers, as their larvae can be parasitic. Choose live-bearing clams only (such as Corbicula fluminalis and Corbicula fluminea). When doing water changes, be careful how you dispose of the water; if possible do not dump it into drains of any kind, as they can be invasive.
Never release freshwater clams into the wild. Corbicula fluminea has become one of the most successful invasive species worldwide and is listed among the "worst invaders" in Europe.
